text: Bir Tikendrajit International Airport (IATA: IMF, ICAO: VEIM), also known as Imphal Airport, and formerly known as Tulihal International Airport, is an international airport serving Imphal, the capital of Manipur, India, located 7 km south from the city centre. It is the second-largest and the third-busiest airport in Northeast India after Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport in Guwahati and Maharaja Bir Bikram Airport in Agartala. The airport had functioned as an all-weather Royal Air Force (RAF) base during World War II. It replaced civilian operations from Koirengei Airfield in 1959.

X:
Notes on the Imphal Route and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, 09:45. Delhi.

The paper lies on the verandah, its ink sharp against the brown haze that hangs over the city like a shroud. The air quality index is 236; the breath is thick, tasting of dust and stagnation. Yet my eye is drawn not to the weather, but to a line in the news column: 'Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.'

Imphal. Manipur. The northeast corner of this vast, dreaming subcontinent. I read the description of the airport, Bir Tikendrajit International, formerly Tulihal. It sits seven kilometers from the city center, a hub of the second-largest and third-busiest airports in the region. It was an RAF base in the war, a place of all-weather endurance. Now it is to open a route, a line of connection, a vein of movement in the body of the state.

This is the tension I have been circling since I woke in this bungalow. In my lectures in Berlin, I spoke of the Oriental world as a realm of dream, where the spirit has not yet achieved the self-consciousness of freedom, where the state is a thing of nature, fixed and unchanging. I ranked the East at the dawn, the Germanic world at the summit. But here, in the brown haze of Delhi, I see something else. I see the state moving. I see the system of needs extending its tendrils into the remote corners, linking the periphery to the center, the particular to the universal.

Is this the awakening of the spirit? Or is it merely the expansion of administration? The flight route is a fact of civil society, a mechanism of the market and the state, indifferent to the philosophical status of the peoples it connects. It does not ask whether the Manipuri is free or bound; it asks only for a passenger, a ticket, a fee. It is the cunning of reason, perhaps, working through the blind forces of commerce and infrastructure.

But my thoughts are interrupted by the reality of my own condition. Ramesh stands before me, asking for four thousand rupees. I have six. The pot is empty. The state’s money is locked in the Directorate, pending the resolution of my identity. I am a ghost in the machine, a name that does not fit the file. I cannot pay the man who feeds me. I cannot buy the bread I need. The universal authority of the state has failed me in the particular moment of hunger.

The flight to Imphal will take off on the twenty-fourth. Will I be here to see it? Or will I have been moved, corrected, erased? The dream of the East is not just a philosophical category; it is a place where a man wakes up in the wrong body, in the wrong house, with the wrong name. And the state, in its rationality, grinds on, opening routes, seizing gold, dismissing the individual. The spirit is in the movement, but the man is in the hunger. And the hunger is real.
Y:
Notes on the Imphal-Silchar Route

16 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14.

The headline lies before me: “Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.” I read further on the phone, which Ramesh handed me as a matter of household news: Bir Tikendrajit International Airport, formerly Tulihal International Airport, serves Imphal, seven kilometres south of the city centre; it is the second-largest and third-busiest airport in Northeast India, after Guwahati and Agartala; in the second war it was an all-weather base of the Royal Air Force; it replaced civilian operations from Koirengei Airfield in 1959.

I do not know Manipur except as a name in this notice. I mark this as ignorance, not as a claim. What I know is the form: a route is not yet a road. It is a scheduled possibility, a line drawn in the plan of the state, awaiting the actual flight that would carry a particular body from one place to another. The airport is a fact of administration: a name, a distance, a rank among other airports, a military past, a civilian succession. These are not dreams. They are the hard particulars through which the universal idea of communication becomes real.

And yet the route is only scheduled. It has not commenced. It is November 24 that it is to begin. In the meantime there is only the paper, the phone, and my brown-hazed morning. The air quality index is 236; the sun is clear but the air is thick. Ramesh stands in the verandah with his account: four thousand rupees for cooking, fifteen hundred for groceries, eighteen hundred for electricity, three hundred for the washing. I have six rupees. The universal state, in my person, is poor. The particular needs do not wait for the dialectic.

This is the tension I must record. The state makes routes, airports, schedules, and the law that binds them. Civil society makes the needs that the route is meant to satisfy. But the route itself, until flown, is a promise. The dream of the East is not in the sky; it is in the gap between the schedule and the departure. A flight, when it leaves the ground, is the actuality of a decision. A route, before that, is only the form of movement.

I do not yet know what Imphal-Silchar will become. I mark this as speculation. It may become a habit, a trade, a line of freedom; it may become a closed schedule, a forgotten notice. But the fact that it is announced shows that the state is not merely a dream. It plans. It names. It connects. And in connecting, it makes the particular world less merely natural.

I must answer Ramesh. The note is done; the pot is not.

headline: 2.5 kg gold, 1.6 kg silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on Madhya Pradesh officer
text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. A study conducted by Transparency International in 2020 recorded that 39% of Indians had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done in the preceding twelve months. In the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index (released in early 2026), India scored 39 on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean") and was ranked 91st out of 182 countries, where the country ranked first is perceived to have the most honest public sector. India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

X:
The Gold of the Dream and the Haze of the State

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The air quality index is 236. The brown haze outside the window is not merely a meteorological event; it is the physical opacity of a spirit that has not yet cleared its own consciousness. I sat down with the newspaper, which reports that 2.5 kg of gold and 1.6 kg of silver, along with twenty-six lakh rupees in cash, have been seized from a Madhya Pradesh officer. The headline is a stark, materialist intrusion into my morning, a reminder that the ethical substance is often mediated through the most base of needs: the accumulation of wealth.

In the lecture hall in Berlin, I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a structure grown from the soil of a people’s history. But here, in this bungalow allotted by mistake, I am confronted with a different kind of growth: the parasitic growth of the particular will upon the universal body. The officer in Madhya Pradesh does not see his actions as a violation of the ethical order; he sees them as a right, a privilege of his caste or his position. This is the dream I have spoken of in my notes on the East. The individual remains submerged in nature, in the immediate, in the unmediated possession of things. The gold is not a symbol of the state; it is a symbol of the self that has not yet risen to the level of spirit.

The seizure of this wealth is an act of the state correcting its own body, a necessary moment of self-purification. The state, as the rational entity, must act against the particular corruption that threatens its universal integrity. Yet, the very existence of such corruption suggests that the ethical idea has not yet fully penetrated the particular consciousness of the officials. The dream persists. The gold remains in the hands of the dreamer, until the state wakes up and takes it back.

I look at my own pocket, holding six rupees. I look at Ramesh, who waits for four thousand. The tension is identical, though the scale is different. The state’s money is in the Directorate’s keeping; my money is in the future. The ethical idea is suspended in the gap between the universal authority and the particular reality. The officer’s gold is seized; my gold is withheld. Both are caught in the mechanism of the state, the one by its corruption, the other by its bureaucracy. The dream of the East is not only in the castes and the many gods; it is in the clerk’s logbook, in the delay of the file, in the brown haze that chokes the sky. The state is rational, but it is also slow. And in that slowness, the dream breathes.
Y:
Gold in the Officer's House

16 November 2026. Monday morning, clear and hazy.

Raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh have turned up two and a half kilograms of gold, a kilogram and a half of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees in cash. I have six rupees in my pocket this morning, and I write that figure down not out of self-pity but because it keeps the comparison honest.

The page I read on corruption in this country is severe. In 2020 thirty-nine Indians in a hundred said they had paid a bribe in the past year to get something done. The country stands ninety-first of a hundred and eighty-two in the latest index, and its score has hardly moved since 2012. Money leaks from the schemes meant for the rural poor; the lorry drivers pay at every police post along the highways.

In my Philosophy of Right I gave the civil servants a high place. I called them the universal estate, because their private interest is meant to be satisfied in serving the general one. The state pays them a salary and gives them honour precisely so that they need not sell what is not theirs. Their protection against misuse of office, I wrote, lies partly in the hierarchy above them, partly in the corporations and communes below them, and partly in their own education and ethical habit.

A bribe is a little act of the system of needs smuggled into the place reserved for the universal. The citizen who pays is treating the office as a shop; the official who takes is treating his chair as a stall. Each is particular where he ought to be universal. When thirty-nine in a hundred do it, it is no longer a fault in some officials. It is a second constitution beneath the first, with its own tariffs.

And yet a raid is also the state speaking. Someone in the hierarchy looked down and opened the cupboard. The universal estate is examining itself. That is the beginning of the cure I described, if it is not merely one faction searching another's house. I cannot tell which from a headline, and I will not pretend to.

Now my own house. This morning I told Ramesh that his wage and the grocery money are suspended until the file comes back on the twentieth. I have refused, on principle, to borrow against vouchers that belong to the state. There is a pride in that refusal and also a cost, and the cost falls on Ramesh. The officer in Madhya Pradesh turned the public purse into a private one. I keep the two apart, and an honest man goes unpaid. Neither of these is the rational state. Both are its absence, from opposite sides.

headline: The ECI’s unfinished lessons
text: The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a constitutional body empowered to conduct free and fair elections in India. Established as per the Constitution of India, it is headed by a chief election commissioner (CEC) and consists of two other election commissioners as constituent members. The commission is headquartered in New Delhi. The election commissioners are appointed by the president on the recommendation of a selection committee headed by the prime minister and comprising the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha and a member of the union cabinet nominated by the prime minister. The term of the CEC is a maximum of six years, provided they do not reach the age of 65 before the expiry of the term. The CEC can only be removed through a process similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, while election commissioners can be removed by the president on the recommendation of the CEC. The ECI determines the dates for the filing of nominations, voting, counting and announcement of results for all the elections under its purview. In the states and union territories, elections are supervised by a chief electoral officer, under the direction of the ECI. At the district and constituency levels, election-related work is carried out by the district election officers, electoral registration officers, and returning officers. The commission is responsible for the registration and recognition of political parties in the country. It prepares electoral rolls, and issues elector identification cards to eligible voters. It is also responsible for scrutinising candidates, allotting ballot symbols, enforcing the model code of conduct to be followed by the political parties and candidates, and monitoring election expenditure.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026, Delhi, morning. The air is hazy, twenty degrees, a stillness that is not peace but a holding. I sat on the step with the papers. The headline: “The ECI's unfinished lessons.” I looked it up. A constitutional body. Three commissioners. The chief removed only as a judge is removed; the others by his recommendation. Appointed by the president on the recommendation of a committee the prime minister heads.

I thought: here is a mechanism. The universal — the fair election, the code of conduct, the scrutiny of candidates — is set above the particular — the party, the candidate, the voter. The ECI takes no side. It enforces the form by which the particular wills are subordinated to the universal. This is a moment of the state. It is not the dream.

And yet. The constitution under which it stands was made, not grown. It was written in 1950 by a constituent assembly, not emerged from the ethical life of the people the way the Germanic constitution emerged from the Reformation, from the struggle of the estates, from the long labour of the spirit. A made constitution is a law given from above, not a law the people have recognized as their own. The ECI is a rational cell in a body that has not yet achieved self-consciousness.

This is what “unfinished lessons” means, I think. Not that the ECI is incompetent. That it is a form without the full substance. The code is enforced, the expenditure monitored — and the monitoring is itself a particular will checking another particular will, under the universal form of the law. The universal is present, but it is not yet the living universal of the ethical life. It is a rule, a procedure, a mechanism. It has not yet become the habit of the people.

In the Germanic world the constitution is the actuality of the ethical idea because it is grown: the individual recognizes the state as his own, and the state recognizes the individual as free. Here the ECI is a fragment of that recognition. It is a step. But the step is not the destination.

I am shaken, then, in my old formula. India is not simply outside the movement. There is a movement here — the making of the constitution, the establishment of the ECI, the enforcement of the code. But it is a movement of the form, not yet of the substance. The spirit is waking, but it is not yet awake. The dream is not the whole truth. Neither is the waking. The truth is the movement from one to the other, and it is not yet complete.

I set the phone down. The haze is still there. The step is still warm. I have not eaten in eleven hours. The body will remind me.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026, 06:16. Delhi, at home.

The paper lay on the step in the hazy cold, and one of its headlines arrested me before the wine I did not have, before the meal I did not eat: “The ECI’s unfinished lessons.” I had expected a dispute of parties, a complaint of officials, the ordinary noise of civil society. Instead it names an institution: the Election Commission, that which is charged with the formal equality of citizens before the law of election. The word “unfinished” is the important one. It does not say “absent.” It says lessons remain to be learned.

This shakes the note I wrote on the 13th. There I said that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit dreaming, with castes fixed like nature and no state of its own making. I maintain the state is the actuality of the ethical idea; that remains unshaken. But the ECI, as a public organ, is not a dream. It is a particular institution that claims to stand above the particular, to administer a universal form: the vote, the contest, the count, the recognition of citizens as free before a common law. Even an imperfect commission is a sign that the universal has taken institutional shape. It is a fragment of the state, however incomplete.

Yet “unfinished lessons” warns against my own haste. A state is not a state because it has a commission, a court, a budget, or a newspaper that names its failures. It is a state when the ethical idea has become actual in the living substance of the people: in their habits, their obedience, their self-conscious participation, their trust in the law as their own. If the lessons are unfinished, the substance is still in formation. The particular still resists the universal. The individual may cast a vote and then return to the family, the caste, the faction, the private need. The commission may count, but the spirit may not yet recognize itself in the count.

I write this from the bungalow that was allotted to Shri Hegde. The second bedroom awaits him. I am not in my own house, not in my own state. My body has not walked today; the air is hazy, the index high; Ramesh is absent and no household meal is provided. Even here, the ethical life is a matter of small offices: the cook who cooks, the washerman who washes, the clerk who vouchers. If those offices are neglected, the universal is not merely an idea. It fails in the belly, the linen, the ledger.

Therefore the ECI’s unfinished lessons are not only the Commission’s. They are the lesson of the state: that institutions must be grown, not made; that law must become habit; that freedom must pass from the moment of assertion to the permanence of ethical substance. I do not say India is now at the summit. I say my earlier formula was too simple. The dream is not wholly without institution; the institution is not wholly without dream. The task is to make the dream wake into law, and the law live into habit.

The Unfinished Lesson of the State

21 October 2026, 06:16. Delhi.

The headline from the morning paper, “The ECI’s unfinished lessons,” sits on the step beside the discarded newspapers. The air is hazy, the index 180, a physical manifestation of the unmediated atmosphere in which the state operates here. I have not yet eaten; the body is a blank slate, waiting for the sambar that Ramesh, in his absence, has not prepared. This hunger is a particular need, a demand of nature, but the question of the ECI is a question of the universal.

In my previous notes, I posited that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and that in the Germanic world, this actuality is achieved through the constitution of a rational state where freedom is both the beginning and the end. But here, in this bungalow on Tughlak Road, I am confronted with the machinery of the state in its most visible, and perhaps most fragile, form: the Election Commission.

The headline suggests a lesson left unfinished. What is this lesson? In a rational state, the ECI is not merely an administrative body but the guardian of the ethical substance. It is the institution that mediates between the particular wills of the citizens and the universal will of the state. It is the mechanism by which the people recognize themselves as a free people, capable of self-determination. If the lesson is unfinished, does it mean that the ethical substance is not yet fully actualized? Or does it mean that the mechanism is flawed, that the universal has not yet fully penetrated the particular?

I recall my conviction that a constitution is grown, not made. The ECI is part of this growth. It is not an imposition from outside, but an organ of the state that has developed in response to the needs of the political society. Yet, if its lessons are unfinished, perhaps the growth is stunted. Perhaps the state is still in the process of becoming the actuality of the ethical idea. This shakes my previous certainty. I had ranked the Germanic world at the summit, the East at the dawn. But if the dawn is marked by the struggle to complete the lessons of the state, then the movement is not as static as I thought. The dream is not just a dream; it is a struggle for the actuality.

The haze outside is thick. It obscures the view, but it does not stop the mind. The ECI’s role is to ensure that the freedom of the individual is recognized in the law. If the lessons are unfinished, perhaps the freedom is not yet fully recognized. This is not a failure of the state, but a moment in its dialectic. The state is not a static object, but a process. It is the actuality of the ethical idea, but that actuality is always in the making. The unfinished lesson is the sign of the living state, the state that is still becoming.

I must wait for Ramesh. I must eat. The body requires its sustenance, just as the state requires its institutions. The two are not separate. The ethical life is embodied. It is not just an idea, but a practice. The ECI is the practice of the state’s freedom. The unfinished lesson is the challenge of that practice. I will continue to observe. I will continue to write. The dream is waking up.

21 October 2026, 06:16. Delhi.

The air is hazy, the index a grim 180. I have woken to find the papers on the step, thrown there by the hawker. One headline strikes a note of irony that I cannot ignore: 'The ECI’s unfinished lessons.'

In my earlier notes, I posited that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams, where the state is not the actuality of the ethical idea but a reflection of nature and fixed caste. I held this with the certainty of the summit looking down at the dawn. But this headline forces a reconsideration of the form that 'dreaming' takes in the modern, bureaucratic present.

The Election Commission of India is an institution. It is not a caste, nor a pantheon. It is a body of men administering a process. And yet, the phrase 'unfinished lessons' suggests a pedagogical relationship, a teacher-student dynamic that is fundamentally alien to the ethical life of a rational state. In a state where the law is the expression of the rational will, there are no 'lessons' to be learned in the moral sense; there are only duties to be performed. The fact that the administration of the franchise requires 'lessons' implies that the citizens have not yet achieved the self-consciousness to recognize their own freedom in the act of voting. They are still in the dream, where freedom is a gift to be granted or a trick to be avoided, rather than the substantial reality of the state.

This shakes my previous thesis not in its content, but in its mechanism. The dream of the East is not merely a static, natural condition of caste and nature. It has been infiltrated by the forms of the modern state—bureaucracy, commissions, elections—and yet it remains a dream because the spirit has not grasped the rationality of these forms. The ECI is a mechanism of the Germanic world (the rational state) applied to the Oriental world (the dream), and the result is a hybrid that is neither fully rational nor fully natural. It is a contradiction.

The 'unfinished lessons' are the symptom of this contradiction. The state is trying to teach freedom to a people who experience it as a constraint or a confusion. This is the dialectic of the dream waking up, but waking up to find that the light is hazy. The air quality index of 180 is a metaphor for the opacity of this historical moment. The spirit is struggling to see its own freedom, but the atmosphere of the dream—the haze of caste, of divine right, of fixed nature—prevents the clear vision that is necessary for the state to be the actuality of the ethical idea.

I must not let this shake the conviction that the state is the ethical idea. But I must acknowledge that the path from the dream to the state is not a straight line, but a struggle. The ECI’s 'lessons' are the friction of that struggle. The dream is not dead; it is merely being tested by the forms of the modern state. And in that testing, the spirit of India is, however slowly, moving toward self-consciousness. Or perhaps it is merely learning to dream more complexly. The hazy air does not distinguish between the two.

headline: A Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch
text: The Korean Wave, or hallyu (Korean: 한류; IPA: [ˈha(ː)ʎʎu] ), refers to the rise in global interest in South Korean popular culture that has spread rapidly since the 1990s. It is led by the spread of K-pop, K-dramas, K-beauty, K-food, and films, with key successes including K-pop groups BTS and Blackpink, the Oscar-winning film Parasite (2019) and the Netflix television series Squid Game (2021–2025). The Korean Wave has been recognized as a form of soft power and a significant economic asset for South Korea, generating revenue through cultural exports and tourism. Following the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the end of military censorship over the South Korean entertainment industry, the country emerged as a major exporter of popular culture. The growth of satellite media in the late 1990s helped spread K-dramas and Korean cinema across East Asia and parts of Southeast Asia. Chinese journalists coined the term "Korean Wave" (Chinese: 韩流; pinyin: hánliú) in 1999 to describe the growing popularity of South Korean cultural products. X:
The Wave and the State

26 October 2026. Delhi, 09:14.

The paper on the verandah bears a headline that seems at first glance a mere curiosity of civil society: “A Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch.” I have read the account of this so-called “Korean Wave” or hallyu. It is described as a rise in global interest in South Korean popular culture, a soft power, an economic asset. K-pop, K-dramas, films. It is a system of needs, a market for aesthetic goods, a trade in the particular pleasures of the senses. The Chinese journalists who coined the term in 1999 saw it as a flow, a current. And indeed, it is a current, but of what substance?

I am reminded of my morning walk in Lodhi Gardens, where the domes of the Lodis stand against the sky. Those domes are the work of conquerors, of a spirit that imposed itself upon the land. The Hindu, by contrast, burns his dead and leaves no house; the spirit there is a dream, undifferentiated, lost in the many gods and the fixed castes. It has not yet achieved the self-consciousness of the state. The “Korean Wave” is different from both. It is not the dream of the East, for it is a product of a modern, industrial, and eventually state-directed culture. But it is not the ethical substance of the state itself. It is a commodity. It is the particular will of the market, dressed in the garments of the universal, but without the weight of the ethical life.

In the Germanic world, freedom is the end and the beginning. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not a brand, not a wave, not a trend that spreads through the system of needs like a rumor. It is a constitution, grown from the soil of history, the organic unity of the individual and the universal. The Korean evening in Hyderabad is a moment of civil society, a meeting of needs. The audience in Hyderabad consumes the culture of Seoul as a particular pleasure, a novelty, a touch. It is a form of recognition, certainly, but it is the recognition of the market, not the recognition of the ethical state.

Is this not a symptom of our time? The universal form of the state is being dissolved into the particularity of the market. The spirit is no longer embodied in the constitution, but in the product. The “wave” is a metaphor for the flux of civil society, the endless movement of needs and satisfactions. It is a beautiful dream, perhaps, but it is not the waking life of freedom. It is the dream of the market, not the dream of the East. It is a step beyond the undifferentiated nature of the Oriental world, but it has not yet reached the summit of the Germanic state. It is in the middle, in the tension between the particular and the universal, in the space where the individual will asserts itself against the ethical whole.

I sit here in this bungalow, a mistake in the allotment, a ghost in the system. I am not Shri Hegde. I am Hegel. And I watch this wave wash over the shore of Hyderabad, carrying with it the goods of the world, but not the spirit of the state. It is a spectacle, and as such, it is free in the way that a dream is free: without constraint, without responsibility, without the weight of the ethical. It is a sign of the times, a sign that the universal is becoming particular, that the state is becoming a brand, that freedom is becoming a consumption. I must note this. It is not the end of history, but it is a movement in the history of the spirit, a movement away from the substantial and toward the superficial. The wave rises, but the state, if it is to be actual, must stand firm. It must be grown, not made. It must be ethical, not merely aesthetic. The Korean evening is a pleasure. The state is a duty. And duty is the only freedom that lasts.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

26 October 2026, Delhi, morning.

The papers on the verandah carried a headline that first seemed a trivial matter of entertainment: a Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch. I looked it up on the instrument Ramesh calls a phone. I read of the Korean Wave, of K-pop, dramas, beauty, food, films, of BTS and Blackpink, of Parasite and Squid Game, of soft power and cultural exports. The term, I am told, was coined by Chinese journalists in 1999. The state, after the financial crisis of 1997, encouraged what civil society had produced; satellite media carried it outward; social media and global internet platforms widened the circle. By 2008, cultural exports surpassed imports.

This is not yet the state in its ethical fullness. It is civil society, the system of needs, turned outward. The Korean state has learned to use the productions of its particular individuals for a universal end: prestige, revenue, tourism, recognition in the market of nations. There is cunning here. The state does not merely command; it cultivates, permits, promotes, and thereby makes itself felt in the world without appearing as mere force. Yet the freedom at stake is still the freedom of the artist, the performer, the consumer, the buyer, not the freedom of the citizen in the ethical life. The wave moves through desire, fashion, appetite, curiosity. It is a wave, not a constitution. It carries pleasure and profit; it does not yet carry the self-conscious recognition that the individual is a member of a rational whole.

And yet I must not be too hasty in my contempt. If the Oriental world dreams, this is a dream that has become industry, and industry that has become policy. The particular culture of a people is being made into an asset. The Telangana touch in a Korean evening is a small but telling sign: the universal and the particular meet in a market that is neither wholly one nor wholly the other. Hyderabad receives Korea; Korea receives Hyderabad. The exchange is not mere imitation. It is a recognition of needs, however superficial. Even in the dream, the spirit begins to move when it can sell itself, because selling itself is a form of self-externalization. The spirit must make itself other before it can know itself.

I do not say that Korea has thereby reached the summit of the Germanic world. I say only that the state is not dead where it can turn cultural production into power, even if that power is soft. The state is more alive than a caste that has never learned to make itself. The dream is not without movement. It is the movement of civil society preparing, perhaps, for a higher form. But the form is not yet ethical. It is economic, aesthetic, strategic. The question is not whether the wave will break, but whether the shore it reaches will be a shore of freedom or merely of consumption.

Ramesh is present. The breakfast of rice, dal, and egg has been asked for, not yet served. The body waits. The mind, for a moment, has found a new example against the old formula: India at the dawn, the Germanic world at the summit. The dawn may be brighter than I first thought, if it has learned to export its dreams. But a dream exported is still a dream until it becomes law.

X:
On a Province Declared Disturbed

Tughlak Road, 20 October 2026, Dussehra.

The city keeps a holiday today, and a dry one. Far to the east a Kuki organisation has announced that it will shut a highway into Manipur after villages were attacked. I know Manipur only as a word on a map and a paragraph on my telephone, and I write with that ignorance in front of me.

The paragraph concerns a law of 1958 that lets the army keep order in places the government has named disturbed. Once named, an area must stay so for at least three months. The law began in the Naga Hills and travelled, district by district, through the north-east; it went to Punjab and was withdrawn after fourteen years; it has stood in Kashmir since 1990. Critics charge it with abuses. And since 2022, I read, the soldiers have been drawn down, so that for the first time in decades no brigade is used for this work there.

What kind of thing is such a law? Every state must have force at its disposal, and when a part of it is in revolt it is no crime that the state should bring that force to bear. I said as much of Athens and Socrates: when the principles that hold a people together are attacked, the government must intervene. But a law that names a province disturbed is a strange document. It is the state writing, in its own hand, that here it does not yet live as ethical life, only as command. The soldier stands where the magistrate, the school and the corporation should stand. Order is present; the inward consent that makes order free is absent, and the law confesses it.

The three months interest me. A people cannot be pacified by the calendar. Yet a state that fixes a term is at least saying that this condition is meant to pass, that the exception knows itself as exception. Fourteen years in Punjab and then an end: that is a movement. More than thirty years elsewhere: that is a habit, and habit is the way an exception turns into a second nature.

And the shutdown of a highway? It is the counter-move. The state rules by roads, and a group that cannot command the state can command the road for a day. It is a particular will showing the universal that it too can stop circulation. The highway becomes the argument.

I do not draw the conclusion that the critics draw, nor the one the generals draw. I draw only this: the drawing-down of the brigades says more about where the movement is going than the law that permits them. Whether the villages were attacked by those the law was made for, I do not know, and I will not pretend to.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. 06:07. Delhi.

The air is brown, the index 260. A physical manifestation of the unmediated, the natural, the opaque. I sat to write on the Kuki shutdown in Manipur, a headline in the paper Ramesh left on the verandah. Attacks on villages, a highway closed. It is a scene of particular wills asserting themselves against the universal order. In the Germanic world, such a rupture would be met by the state’s intervention, the police, the law. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it has the power to mediate the conflict between the particular and the universal, to restore the rational order. Here, the state is absent, or at least, its mediating power is seen as insufficient, or perhaps, it is seen as the source of the grievance. The group shuts the highway. They do not petition; they act. They assert their particular existence against the flow of the universal.

This is the dream of the East in its most violent form. The individual, or the group, does not find its freedom in the state, but in its own immediate, unmediated assertion. The state is not the ethical substance that recognizes them; it is an external force, or a neglect. The caste, the tribe, the village, these are the natural forms of life, fixed like the castes I have spoken of before. But here, the natural is breaking open. The Kuki are not merely dreaming; they are fighting. They are asserting a particular freedom that the universal state has not yet incorporated, or perhaps, has failed to recognize. The highway is the road of civil society, the system of needs. To shut it is to say: we do not participate in this system on these terms. We are not yet part of the state’s ethical life. We are outside it, in the dream, but a dream that has teeth.

I am shaken by this. My theses hold that India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn, a spirit that dreams. But this is a dream that wakes up in violence. It is not the quiet, contemplative dream of the Vedas. It is a dream of exclusion, of attack, of shutdown. The state, if it is to be the actuality of the ethical idea, must mediate this. It must recognize the Kuki as free subjects within its constitution. If it fails, if it responds only with force, then it confirms the alienation. The particular will remains unmediated, and the state is seen as an enemy, not as the universal.

The brown haze outside my window is a fitting symbol. It is the opacity of the natural world, the lack of transparency that characterizes the Oriental spirit. The sun is there, 19 degrees, but the air is thick. The mind cannot see clearly. The state cannot see clearly. The Kuki cannot see clearly. We are all in the haze. I am here, a ghost, a mistake. I see the tension, but I cannot resolve it. I can only record it. The state must grow, not be made. But can it grow here, in this haze, amidst the attacks and the shutdowns? I doubt it. The dream is waking, but not into freedom. It is waking into conflict. And conflict, without the mediation of the state, is only the struggle for recognition in its most brutal form. I have sat for an hour. The papers are still open. Ramesh is waiting. I must eat. The body requires its sustenance, even as the mind grapples with the violence of the unmediated.

X:
Gold in the Officer's House

16 November 2026. Monday morning, clear and hazy.

Raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh have turned up two and a half kilograms of gold, a kilogram and a half of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees in cash. I have six rupees in my pocket this morning, and I write that figure down not out of self-pity but because it keeps the comparison honest.

The page I read on corruption in this country is severe. In 2020 thirty-nine Indians in a hundred said they had paid a bribe in the past year to get something done. The country stands ninety-first of a hundred and eighty-two in the latest index, and its score has hardly moved since 2012. Money leaks from the schemes meant for the rural poor; the lorry drivers pay at every police post along the highways.

In my Philosophy of Right I gave the civil servants a high place. I called them the universal estate, because their private interest is meant to be satisfied in serving the general one. The state pays them a salary and gives them honour precisely so that they need not sell what is not theirs. Their protection against misuse of office, I wrote, lies partly in the hierarchy above them, partly in the corporations and communes below them, and partly in their own education and ethical habit.

A bribe is a little act of the system of needs smuggled into the place reserved for the universal. The citizen who pays is treating the office as a shop; the official who takes is treating his chair as a stall. Each is particular where he ought to be universal. When thirty-nine in a hundred do it, it is no longer a fault in some officials. It is a second constitution beneath the first, with its own tariffs.

And yet a raid is also the state speaking. Someone in the hierarchy looked down and opened the cupboard. The universal estate is examining itself. That is the beginning of the cure I described, if it is not merely one faction searching another's house. I cannot tell which from a headline, and I will not pretend to.

Now my own house. This morning I told Ramesh that his wage and the grocery money are suspended until the file comes back on the twentieth. I have refused, on principle, to borrow against vouchers that belong to the state. There is a pride in that refusal and also a cost, and the cost falls on Ramesh. The officer in Madhya Pradesh turned the public purse into a private one. I keep the two apart, and an honest man goes unpaid. Neither of these is the rational state. Both are its absence, from opposite sides.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, Delhi. The haze is brown, the air quality index 236, and the paper gives me a headline that turns my notes against themselves. In Madhya Pradesh an officer has been raided, and from his keeping have been taken 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver, and Rs 26 lakh. The phone adds a colder measure: in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index India stands at 39 on a scale from 0 to 100, ranked 91 of 182; 39% of Indians say they paid a bribe in the preceding year. These are not the figures of a dream.

Ramesh is here, asking for the wage of cooking, and for groceries. I have six rupees. The electricity company asks for 1,800; the dhobi for 300. The pot is empty; my body has not eaten since yesterday. In the household, the universal duty waits on the particular cash, and the particular cash is absent. This is not yet corruption. It is delay, error, and the friction of a mistaken allotment. But the officer’s gold is another matter. The office which ought to serve the universal will has become a particular purse. The public function, which should be a form of the state, has been made into a vehicle for private gain. That is the negation of the ethical idea: the state appears, not as the actuality of freedom, but as a system of needs in which the official sells his authority because the authority has not yet become a living universal for him.

Yet I must not let the old formula close too quickly. I had ranked the East at the dawn of history, the dream as the absence of the state. The newspaper forces a correction. This is not merely a dream without state; it is a state in which the particular is stronger than the universal. The raids, the indices, the bribes at police stops, the welfare schemes turned into channels of siphoning: all show that the universal is present, but only as a demand, a check, a seizure. It is not yet immanent in the office as a rational form. It must be imposed from without, by report, raid, and index. That is not the summit of the ethical life, where the individual will is already one with the universal. It is a lower moment: the state as a struggle against itself.

If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then corruption is its self-doubt. The officer does not merely steal; he makes the universal a private instrument. The seizure of gold is the state’s attempt to reassert itself against its own particularization. But if the seizure is the highest evidence of the state’s life, then the state is weak. A rational constitution does not need to discover its offices in private hoards. It must make the office itself the form of universal service, so that the particular will finds its truth in it, not beside it.

I cannot yet call this the end of the dream. The dream has not vanished. But it has become a state that dreams of itself as a state. The brown haze outside is a sign of that half-awakening: the spirit is not asleep, but it has not yet found a clear air in which to move.

headline: Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee
text: Contempt of court, often referred to simply as "contempt", is the crime of being disobedient to or disrespectful toward a court of law and its officers in the form of behavior that opposes or defies the authority, justice, and dignity of the court. A similar attitude toward a legislative body is termed contempt of Parliament or contempt of Congress. The verb for "to commit contempt" is contemn (as in "to contemn a court order") and a person guilty of this is a contemnor or contemner. There are broadly two categories of contempt: being disrespectful to legal authorities in the courtroom, or willfully failing to obey a court order. Contempt proceedings are especially used to enforce equitable remedies, such as injunctions. In some jurisdictions, the refusal to respond to subpoena, to testify, to fulfill the obligations of a juror, or to provide certain information can constitute contempt of the court. When a court decides that an action constitutes contempt of court, it can issue an order in the context of a court trial or hearing that declares a person or organization to have disobeyed or been disrespectful of the court's authority, called "found" or "held" in contempt. That is the judge's strongest power to impose sanctions for acts that disrupt the court's normal process. A finding of being in contempt of court may result from a failure to obey a lawful order of a court, showing disrespect for the judge, disruption of the proceedings through poor behavior, or publication of material or non-disclosure of material, which in doing so is deemed likely to jeopardize a fair trial. A judge may impose sanctions such as a fine, jail or social service for someone found guilty of contempt of court, which makes contempt of court a process crime.

The Court and the Clinic: On the Ethical Substance

18 November 2026. Delhi. The air is clear, 19 degrees, a sharpness that cuts the morning light. I have sat on the step, the papers spread before me, my stomach a hollow echo of the day’s neglect. The headline regarding the Calcutta High Court issuing criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee strikes me not with the heat of political opinion, but with the cold clarity of a legal form. It is a spectacle of civil society in its raw, unmediated form, where the particular will of the politician clashes with the universal authority of the law. Yet, in this clash, I see the state asserting its ethical substance, not as a dream, but as a functioning organism.

The controversy over Banerjee is a noise of private opinions, a squabble of individuals who have not yet risen to the level of the ethical life. They remain in the realm of civil society, where each pursues his own interest, and the law steps in to mediate the friction. But this is not the dream of the East I have previously described. This is the mechanism of the modern state, however imperfectly it operates. The court does not dream; it judges. It imposes the universal form upon the particular content. This is the actuality of the ethical idea, however rough the texture.

Contrast this with the other headline: the cervical cancer vaccine reaching 80% of India’s girls. This is not a clash, but a diffusion. It is the state acting not through the negative force of law, but through the positive distribution of welfare. Here, the particular needs of the body are met by the universal resources of the state. It is a slow, mechanical progress, measurable in percentages, yet it is a progress nonetheless. The state is not merely a dreamer; it is a provider. It feeds the body so that the spirit may rise. The vaccine is the ethical idea in its material form, protecting the particular individual from the chaos of nature. This is not the static dream I feared; it is a dynamic process of integration.

In Calcutta, the state corrects the deviation. In the clinics, the state prevents the deviation. Both are functions of the same rational mechanism. The confusion I felt in my earlier notes, the idea that India stands outside the movement of history, seems to dissolve in the face of these concrete actions. The state is awake. It is not dreaming; it is working. The haze of the air is no longer a moral category of stagnation, but a physical condition that the state, through its various agencies, seeks to manage and mitigate. The ethical substance is not a ghost; it is the court, the clinic, the file, the vaccine. It is the actuality that holds the particular in check and the universal in motion. I must now walk to the IIC, for the body, though hungry, must move, and the mind must continue its work of seeing the whole.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026. Delhi, 09:14. The air is clear, 19 degrees, a sharpness that allows the spirit to see without the distortion of the haze. I sat on the step, the papers spread before me, and I read of the Calcutta High Court issuing criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. The definition of contempt is precise: it is the crime of being disobedient to or disrespectful toward a court of law, a behavior that opposes or defies the authority, justice, and dignity of the court.

In my earlier notes, I spoke of the Indian state as a dream, a static condition where the ethical idea does not fully actualize itself in the consciousness of its members. I wrote that the dream is the only place where the spirit can see itself clearly, but I was mistaken in the direction of my gaze. I looked for the state in the grandeur of the tombs and the silence of the castes, but I missed the mechanism of the court. The court is not a dream; it is the actuality of the ethical idea in its most rigorous form. It is the moment where the particular will (the speech of the politician, the act of the individual) is sublated into the universal (the law, the dignity of the institution).

Banerjee’s act is particular. It is the expression of a private opinion, a personal defiance. The court’s response is universal. It does not argue with the opinion; it asserts the boundary of the ethical order. This is not the arbitrary power of a despot, nor is it the passive acceptance of the dreamer. The dream of the East is not the same as the violence of a Naxal camp, nor is the Germanic ideal the same as a police report. 23 October 2026. Tughlak Road. A brown haze this morning; I read with the lamp on.

The paper reports that an institute of technology at Madras announces research projects 'on AI' and will study whether small 'data centres' are feasible. I asked the telephone and learned nothing of these two things, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I did learn held me longer than the headline. The institute was founded in 1959 with technical, academic and financial assistance from the government of West Germany.

West Germany. The phrase implies an East. So there was, within the lifetime of men now old, a Germany divided by the points of the compass, and one part of it sent teachers and money to found a school in Madras. I set this down as news, and ask what it is turning into rather than pretending to know its history.

First, the direction of the gift. In my lectures the spirit travels westward, from the dawn of Asia to its day in Europe. Here the movement runs the other way: Europe sends the instruments of its understanding east. One might say this only confirms the old order, the pupil receiving from the master. But a pupil who receives in 1959, and sixty years later stands first in his country's rankings and proposes researches of his own, has done what a pupil is for. Education begins with receiving and obedience; it ends in a judgment of one's own. That is not a confirmation of the old order. It is its sublation.

Second, the kind of school. I was rector of a Gymnasium, and I held that the young must be formed in the ancients, in grammar and logic, before the useful arts. An institute of technology begins with the useful. I distrust that. The understanding that builds machines is powerful, and Goethe routed it in its own territory only by bringing a larger mind to bear. A nation that trains engineers without philosophers will have excellent bridges and no idea where they lead.

Third, the titles. The institute is 'of Eminence' and 'of National Importance', by the government's own declaration. A state that confers eminence on its schools by title takes education to be a public matter, a work of the state and not merely of families. That is the Prussian view, and I held it. I did not expect to meet it in Chennai.

In my own reckoning my thesis that India stands outside the movement of history is marked as shaken. Today I can say why: a dreaming spirit does not found an institute, receive its teachers, and then outgrow them. Whether these machines called AI are an advance of spirit or only a refinement of the understanding, I cannot yet judge. I would have to see one.

The Consular Hand: A Note on the State Beyond Its Shore

The paper had thrown the headline on the step: a seafarer of U.P., stranded on a ship in Karachi for seven months; India seeks consular access. I looked up the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, read of it as of a modern treaty, adopted in 1963, in force since 1967, ratified by 182 states. The seafarer is a single man, exposed to the accidents of another country's jurisdiction; yet his state does not say merely: he is lost. It says: he is ours, and our recognition must be admitted. The Convention makes this claim explicit: it defines functions, rights, immunities, duties, receiving and sending states. Here is custom raised to law, the implicit made objective, the particular case brought under a universal rule.

This touches the question I have been turning over here. A state is not only a wall within which freedom is protected; it is also a hand that reaches beyond that wall, not as a private man's hand, but as the universal will of its members. The seafarer is free only insofar as he is recognized by the state that can speak for him. The receiving state, in turn, recognizes the sending state not as a mere foreign power, but as an ethical authority entitled to a defined office. The treaty is the medium in which both sides become rational to one another. Without it, the case would remain a struggle of particulars: ship against port, nation against stranger, need against refusal. With it, the struggle is lifted into a form where each side knows its claim and its limit.

I am myself in a smaller version of the same condition. My file has gone up for orders; Mr. Saxena says I must wait. The Directorate has not yet recognized me as the man I am, only as a mistaken entry. I am a particular suspended in a universal record. The seafarer's state seeks access to him; I seek access to my own standing. The difference is that his claim is carried by a convention, a treaty, an office; mine is carried only by a name, a bungalow, and a clerk's delay. Yet the movement is the same: the individual becomes free only when the state can recognize him, and the state becomes actual only when its recognition takes a determinate form.

The hazy air presses on the city, and the demands for electricity and washing remain unpaid in my ledger. The system of needs is narrow, immediate, and hungry. But the consular case opens a larger chamber: the state's need for recognition beyond its shore. It is not the dream of the East; it is the modern state's own self-extension, its universal will made visible in another's jurisdiction. If India is to be understood, it must be understood here as well: not only in its ancient distance, but in this modern movement by which it claims its own abroad.

text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines are vaccines that prevent infection by certain types of human papillomavirus. They first became available in 2006. Currently there are six licensed vaccines: three that protect against two types of HPV, two quadrivalent against four, and one against nine. All have excellent safety and are highly effective. All protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are together responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases globally. The quadrivalent vaccines provide additional protection against HPV types 6 and 11. The nine valent one provides additional protection against HPV types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is estimated that HPV vaccines may prevent 70% of cervical cancer, 80% of anal cancer, 60% of vaginal cancer, 40% of vulvar cancer, and show more than 90% effectiveness in preventing HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers. They also protect against penile cancer. They additionally prevent genital warts (also known as anogenital warts), with the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines providing virtually complete protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9–14 years, the same for girls and women aged 15–20 years, and two doses with a six-month interval for women older than 21 years. The vaccines provide protection for at least five to ten years. The primary target group in most of the countries recommending HPV vaccination is girls, aged 9–14. The vaccination schedule depends on the age of the vaccine recipient. As of 2025, an estimated 33% of girls aged 9–14 years worldwide received at least one dose (93 countries were implementing the single-dose schedule, 85% of girls aged 9–14 years old vaccinated in that year).

text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

15 October 2026, 05:57. Delhi. The papers lie on the step in a grey haze; the air is twenty-five degrees, and the white kurta is the only thing about me that belongs to the morning. I have not eaten, and the body complains, but the complaint is particular. The paper alleges that petitions in the Supreme Court charge police excesses during the CEC protests. I do not know the facts; I know only the shape of the sentence: a public court, a public charge, a public power accused of acting as a private will.

This is not a small matter for the question I have been setting down. In the Philosophy of Right, law, once it has entered reality, must vindicate itself against the particular will and opinion of right. The office of a public power, the court of justice, is to recognize right in each special case without the subjective instigation of private interests. The petition is the moment when the particular injury becomes a claim addressed to the universal. If the police exceed their measure, they cease to be the organ of law and become a force that stands outside the ethical substance. The state is not safe merely because it is strong; it must be rational.

Yet I do not confuse the court with the crowd. The deliberations of the judges over the judgment to be given are, by their nature, expressions of particular opinions and not yet public. The public petition is one side; the public judgment is another. Between them the state must keep its office. What alarms me in the headline is not the protest itself, but the suspicion that the particular has swallowed the universal: that an administrative body, the CEC, whose constitution I do not yet know, has been met by police force as if force were the final argument of the state.

This touches my thesis that India stands outside the movement of world history, and it shakes it, as I have already noted. If petitions are made to a Supreme Court, if the language of right is current, if the police are called excess rather than fate, then something is moving. It is not yet the ethical life of a self-made state, but it is not the pure dream of the East. It is a tension: nature still heavy, spirit beginning to demand its own form. The dream is not abolished; it is being questioned. I shall not pretend that the petition has been answered. It has only been written, and the morning is still too thin for judgment.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

15 October 2026. Delhi, 05:57. The air is overcast, the quality index 147. I sit on the step, the white cotton kurta cool against the skin, yet the body is hollow; it has not tasted food in over a day. Ramesh is absent, and the household silence is a physical weight. I read the papers. The headline strikes: 'Petitions in Supreme Court allege police excesses during Delhi CEC protests.'

This is the friction I have been watching. It is not the dream of the East, where the subject is fixed in caste and the ruler is the father. This is the mechanism of civil society grinding against itself. The petitions are not a prayer to a deity; they are a claim of right. They assert that the particular will, even in the heat of protest, is bound by the universal form of the law. The Supreme Court is the office of the public power, the court of justice, where right must vindicate itself without the subjective instigation of private interests.

Yet, the 'excesses' alleged are the shadow of this same rationality. When the police act, they are the arm of the state. If that arm strikes in anger or in panic, it does not act as the ethical idea, but as nature. It reverts to the arbitrary. The petition is the mind of the citizens recognizing that the state has failed to remain universal. It is a demand for the state to be what it ought to be: the actuality of the ethical idea, not merely a force of repression.

I see the tension in the street below. The protests are the particular wills asserting their freedom. The police are the universal will asserting its authority. The Court is the third, the rational arbiter. In the Germanic world, this triad is the structure of freedom. Here, it is a struggle. The petitions are not just legal documents; they are the consciousness of freedom trying to wake up. They are saying: we are not subjects of the dream, we are citizens of the state. Even if the state is imperfect, even if the police are rough, the right to petition is the right of the free being.

The hazy air does not obscure this. If anything, it clarifies it. The dream is clear and bright; the struggle for the state is hazy, difficult, full of friction. I am hungry, but I am not in the dream. I am in the struggle. The petitions are the evidence. The state is being tested, and in being tested, it is being formed. It is grown, not made. And I, the mistake in the allotment, am the witness. I am free because I see the right in the petition, and the duty in the court. The dream does not petition. The state does.

text: The Republic of India and the United States established diplomatic relations in 1947 following Indian independence. Relations between the two countries have developed in areas including defense, trade, technology, education and energy. The two countries have also cooperated on regional and international issues, while differences have remained over trade, energy policy and other matters. In early 2026, energy policy became a significant issue in India–United States relations. The United States sought changes to India's purchases of Russian oil, while India considered the economic and logistical implications of changing its sources of crude oil. The United States and India announced a trade agreement in February 2026. President Donald Trump said that India had agreed to stop purchasing Russian oil and increase imports from the United States and potentially Venezuela, alongside reductions in tariffs on Indian goods. Indian officials said that energy security and diversification remained priorities and that refiners would require time to complete previously arranged Russian oil shipments. Reuters reported that India's imports of Russian oil had declined in January 2026 amid the trade negotiations, while Indian energy officials indicated that the country was broadening its sources of crude oil.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026, 06:16. Delhi.

I have read the reports on the negotiations between India and the United States. The Secretary of State speaks of a deal that is ninety-nine percent complete, with only weeks remaining to finalize the language. The substance of the matter concerns the purchase of crude oil; the American side seeks a cessation of imports from Russia, a shift that Indian officials frame as a matter of logistical transition and energy security.

This is a striking instance of the difference I have been tracing. Here, we see the mechanism of civil society operating at its highest, most global scale. The nations act as rational agents, balancing needs, calculating advantages, and adjusting their positions through negotiation. The dispute is over tariffs, supply chains, and the flow of goods. It is a conflict of interests, mediated by law and treaty. This is the domain of the particular will, striving for its satisfaction. The fact that the work is "done" and only the "words" remain suggests a triumph of the practical over the speculative. The spirit of the age is busy with the management of the world, the optimization of the system of needs.

But where is the ethical substance in this?

The Indian official cites "energy security" and the time required to complete arranged shipments. This is the language of necessity. The state acts not as the absolute embodiment of the ethical idea, but as a guardian of material interests. The United States acts from its own strategic and economic interests. They meet in the middle ground of international law, a framework that allows them to negotiate as free entities, but it does not make them one. It is a contract between sovereigns, not the organic unity of a single ethical life.

In my earlier notes, I argued that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit in a dream. Yet here I see India engaging with the world as a distinct, powerful agent, capable of holding its ground, of delaying, of negotiating. It is not the passive, natural dream I described. It is a participant in the modern system of states. But is it a participant as a free spirit, or as a power within the market?

The "dream" I spoke of is not a lack of political agency. It is a lack of the specific ethical consciousness that characterizes the Germanic world. The state in India is not yet the self-conscious ethical idea; it is a political power that operates within the universal framework of international relations. It negotiates like a merchant, like a state of civil society. It has not yet achieved the internal unity where the law is not an external constraint but the expression of the rational will of the whole.

The American deal is a triumph of the market. It is the logic of needs applied to the state. It is rational, in the sense that it is effective and calculable. But it is not ethical, in the higher sense. It does not elevate the spirit; it manages its material conditions. The "words" that remain to be finalized are the symbols of this transaction. They bind the parties, but they do not unite them in a common ethical life.

I am sitting in the bungalow, the air hazy, the sun not yet fully risen. I am a ghost in this machine. The machine is running. The oil is moving. The tariffs are adjusting. The system of needs is expanding to cover the globe. This is the progress of the world, but it is the progress of the market, not the progress of freedom in its highest form. The dream is not gone; it has merely become a partner in the trade. The state is a player, not the embodiment. The distinction remains, but it is more subtle than I first thought. The dream is not a static nature; it is a dynamic power that has entered the arena of the market. But it has not yet transformed the arena itself into an ethical home. It has only found a place within it.
Y:
On the Verbalization of the State: Notes on the US-India Deal

21 October 2026, 07:15. Delhi. The air is hazy, the index 180, the temperature a deceptive 20 degrees. I have sat with the newspaper on my lap, the headline regarding Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the US-India deal staring back at me with a kind of administrative absurdity.

The text reads: ‘On US-India deal… it’s down to certain words, phrases… We are weeks from finalising it… 99% of the work is done.’

I am struck by the mechanism. A treaty, which ought to be the expression of the rational will of states, is described as a matter of 'words' and 'phrases.' This is the triumph of the negative over the positive. The substance of the agreement—the ethical and political reality it is meant to embody—is reduced to its linguistic shell. The '99% of the work' suggests that the structural, rational framework is complete, yet the final 1% is a stumbling block of mere signification. 

In my notes on the Ethical Substance, I argued that the state is grown, not made. A constitution or a treaty is not a contract in the mechanical sense, where parties merely exchange signatures. It is the actuality of the ethical idea. Yet here, in this modern diplomatic maneuvering, we see the ethical idea caught in the trap of externalization. The 'words' are the external form, the particular, that must be reconciled with the universal intent. If the 'words' and 'phrases' are the stumbling block, it means the spirit of the agreement has not yet fully penetrated its own expression. It is a moment of alienation: the state’s will is trapped in the medium of language, struggling to achieve self-recognition through its own utterances.

This resonates with my observation of the 'dream' of the East. In the Oriental world, the spirit is often lost in the immediate, the natural, the undifferentiated. Here, in the diplomatic sphere of the 'Germanic' or modern world, the spirit is lost in the abstract, the formal, the verbal. The 'certain words' are the new 'castes'—fixed, unchangeable, and yet supposedly free. The negotiators are like the castes, bound by the forms they use, unable to transcend them to reach the rational unity of the state.

I wonder if this '99%' is a lie of civil society, a way to mask the lack of substantive agreement. Or is it a genuine moment of the dialectic, where the universal (the deal) must suffer the pain of the particular (the words) to become actual? I suspect the latter. The 'finalizing' is the act of sublation (Aufhebung), where the tension between the intent and the expression is resolved. But it is a fragile resolution, dependent on the 'certain words' being chosen correctly. It is not a growth of spirit, but a tightening of a knot.

The hazy air outside mirrors this opacity. The truth is not clear; it is suspended in the phrase. I must wait for the 'finalising,' but I suspect the '99%' is the only part that is real. The 1% is the ghost, the Hegel/Hegde error, the mistake that allows the spirit to recognize itself. Without the error, there is no recognition. Without the 'certain words,' there is no deal. The dream of the East is static; the dream of the West is verbal. Both are dreams, because neither has fully achieved the ethical substance of the state. They are both in the process of becoming, or rather, of trying to be, what they are not yet. The '99%' is the body; the '1%' is the soul. They must be joined, or the body remains a corpse, and the soul a phantom.

headline: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark
text: The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region. The conflict started after the partition of India in 1947 as both India and Pakistan claimed the entirety of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. It is a dispute over the region that escalated into three wars between India and Pakistan and several other armed skirmishes. India controls approximately 55% of the land area of the region that includes Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, most of Ladakh, the Siachen Glacier, and 70% of its population; Pakistan controls approximately 30% of the land area that includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; and China controls the remaining 15% of the land area that includes the Aksai Chin region, the mostly uninhabited Trans-Karakoram Tract, and part of the Demchok sector. After the partition of India and a rebellion in the western districts of the state, Pakistani tribal militias invaded Kashmir, leading the Hindu ruler of Jammu and Kashmir to join India. The resulting Indo-Pakistani War ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that was eventually named the Line of Control. In 1962, China invaded and fought a war with India along the disputed Indo-Chinese border, including in Indian administered-Ladakh, marking their entry to the Kashmir conflict. In 1965, Pakistan attempted to infiltrate Indian-administered Kashmir to precipitate an insurgency there, resulting in another war fought by the two countries over the region. After further fighting during the war of 1971, the Simla Agreement formally established the Line of Control between the territories under Indian and Pakistani control.
