On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, Delhi, 06:13. Sitting 3.

The papers were left on the verandah by Ramesh, where the first light lay on them before the city had fully woken. I paid him for the groceries, and stood for a moment in my white cotton kurta, the air clear and hazy, the index of the air at 139. The body has not yet received breakfast, and the second bedroom is still empty, pending orders for Shri Hegde. In that empty room, and in the headline, I saw the same problem: a place that belongs to a name, but has not yet been filled by a person.

The headline says: “Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark.” I do not know the full course of the debate, and I do not pretend to it. What I know is the form of the event. One state speaks to another. It claims a territory, asserts a boundary, and demands that the other recognize the claim. This is not the language of nature. It is the language of right. The state has become a subject that can say: this is ours, and you must answer.

This shakes my earlier note that India stands outside the movement of world history. At least, it shakes the old image of a spirit that merely dreams. A dream does not keep a row alive. A dream does not file a claim, publish a newspaper, or pay a caretaker. The row over Kashmir is the row of states, not of castes. It shows the state as an ethical subject, however incomplete. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and here that actuality is visible in the very dispute: a boundary is not a line in the dust, but a demand made by one rational whole to another.

And yet I do not reverse my judgment. The ethical substance is not yet fully grown. The boundary is contested, and a contested boundary is not yet a self-certainty. The state appears, but it appears through division, through accusation, through the need for external recognition. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of freedom because it contains the individual in itself. Here, the individual and the region are still torn from the universal. The row is the form of the state, but the content is still a wound. The dream has not vanished; it has taken the shape of a political claim.

I must therefore amend my thesis. India is not outside the movement of history, as a country outside a road. It is in the movement, but at a point where the state has not yet become the self-conscious ethical idea. It has the form of right, the newspaper, the boundary, the dispute. It has not yet the content of reconciliation. The dream is no longer only the dream of many gods and fixed castes. It is now the dream of a people that has the shape of a state but has not yet found its unity in that state.

The second bedroom waits for Hegde. The row waits for an answer. Both are places where the universal has named itself, but the particular has not yet been received into it. That is the day’s movement. It is not the summit, but it is no longer only the dawn.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, Delhi, 06:13. The papers lay on the verandah; the air is clear, but the index stands at 139, a warning that even the element in which the body breathes is not pure. I paid Ramesh one thousand five hundred rupees for the kitchen; the cash leaves my pocket, and the need is satisfied. This is the small, definite movement of civil society. Before breakfast, I turned to the headline that had struck me: Farooq Abdullah, a name I do not know, is said to have stirred a row by declaring that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I read what the phone gave me as the matter itself: a territorial conflict over Kashmir, begun after the partition of India in 1947, carried on between India and Pakistan, and also, in the north-east, between India and China. It is not a question of doctrine, at least in the first statement, but of land, population, control, and the line by which control is to be held.

What is remarkable is that the dispute has not remained a single event. It has produced wars, ceasefires, a line called the Line of Control, and an agreement at Simla. The particular state of Jammu and Kashmir, once a princely state, has been divided among three powers, each holding a portion. Here the mind sees the state not as a calm ethical substance, but as a power that claims, defends, and reclaims territory. The individual will is no longer the dream of the Oriental world, where freedom remains inside the given; it has become the will of nations, each demanding recognition and each resisting the recognition it gives. The conflict is therefore a moment of right, though a violent and unfinished one. It is the right of the state to exist, to be continuous, to be not merely a name on a map but a body of law, army, and administration.

And yet I do not say that this dispute belongs to the highest movement of world history. It is a territorial contest, and as such it belongs to the necessary but lower form of external right. The ethical idea is not yet at peace with itself; it is divided into states that cannot fully recognize one another. The Line of Control is not a boundary drawn by reason, but a line drawn by force and then preserved by agreement. It is a truce, not a reconciliation. What is turning into here is perhaps a harder form of the same problem: peoples who have been separated by the accident of partition, who now live under different constitutions, and who nevertheless remain entangled in a common past. The dream of the East is not the only dream. The modern world dreams too, in the form of the state that believes its own claim to be complete. The task of reason is to show that no state is the whole of the ethical idea, and that the struggle for recognition must pass beyond territory into law, into mutual right, and finally into a universal order that the phone does not yet name.

The technique is used to quickly and cheaply clear fields. It is still widespread today. Stubble burning has been associated with increasing air pollution over the past few decades due to the particulate matter contamination it distributes into the atmosphere. In India, stubble burning generates a thick haze. These fires pose a significant health risk to individuals across all ages. In countries such as India and Pakistan, stubble burning is illegal. Enforcement is weak, allowing the practice to continue.

X:
The Haze and the Ethical Idea

The brown haze hangs over Delhi today, an index of 302, a physical weight that presses against the glass and the lungs alike. In the paper, I read of 1,152 farm fires in Punjab on Deepavali. Stubble burning. It is a practice of immediate utility: to clear the field, to save time, to satisfy the present need. It is the logic of the particular will, unmediated by the universal. The farmer burns the stubble because it is in the way of the next harvest, because the cost of waiting or of mechanical clearing is too high for the individual. The result is a thick haze that chokes the capital, a pollution that affects all, yet is generated by the many separate acts of the few. It is a contradiction in the flesh: the particular action destroys the universal condition of life.

I have sat with this for an hour. The air in the study is thick, not just with particulate matter, but with the weight of my own position. I am a guest here, a mistake in the records, yet I observe with a clarity that perhaps only the outsider can possess. In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as the dream of the East, a spirit that has not yet reached the summit of freedom. I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, the grown organism that mediates between the individual and the universal. But here, in this haze, I see a different tension. The state claims to be the universal, to be the rational order. Yet, in this instance, it has failed to mediate. The law forbids the burning, yet enforcement is weak. The universal rule is known, but the particular will remains unchecked. The state is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea in this moment; it is a promise that has not yet been fulfilled.

There is a dialectic here that I must not overlook. The haze is a negative moment. It is the destruction of the clear air, the violation of the common space. But it is also a revelation. It reveals the gap between the ideal and the real, between the law on the books and the life on the ground. It shows that the ethical substance is not yet fully formed, that the movement of spirit toward freedom is still in progress, still struggling against the weight of nature and particularity. The farmer is not wrong in his immediate need; he is simply trapped in a stage of development that has not yet achieved the higher unity of particular and universal.

I am hungry. It has been twenty hours since my last meal. Ramesh asks for money for cooking, for groceries. I have only ₹166. The system of needs is immediate, urgent, and indifferent to my philosophical musings. I must pay the dhobi, the electricity, the caretaker. These are the particulars that make up the texture of life. They are not yet elevated into the universal, but they are the material from which the universal is made. I must not despise them. I must engage with them, not as a philosopher above the world, but as a man within it. The haze is outside, but it is also inside, in the lungs, in the mind, in the struggle to think clearly in a world that does not yet think clearly. I will write this down, and then I will face the day, one particular step at a time.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

10 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14. The brown haze is already on the glass, an index of 302, as if the air itself had become a ledger. The paper gives a figure: 1,152 farm fires in Punjab on Deepavali, the season’s biggest single-day jump. I looked up the word on the phone: stubble burning. It is the setting fire to the straw left after rice or wheat, a quick and cheap clearing, widespread, illegal, weakly enforced. The particular is plain: a field must be made ready; labour is scarce or dear; the flame is the cheapest hand. The universal is also plain: the law forbids it, yet the law does not appear in the field as a living power. There is a tension here that disturbs my earlier notes.

I had spoken of the East as a spirit that dreams, castes fixed like nature, no state of its own making. The fire does not prove that India has reached the summit of self-conscious freedom. But it does prove that the picture is not a still picture. The field is not merely a dream; it is a system of needs. The grain, the harvest, the stubble, the law, the haze, the health of the lungs, the festival of lights, the smoke that chokes the city—these are moments in one movement. The farmer does not choose smoke for its beauty; he chooses it because it clears. The state does not merely command; it fails to enforce, and that failure is part of the actual. A law that is written but not actual is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea. It is a universal that has not yet entered the particular.

The festival deepens the contradiction. Deepavali is the festival of lamps, of light against darkness. Yet the greatest day’s fire is not in the house but in the field. The light is meant to be received; the smoke is produced. One is a sign; the other is a labour. In this I see a moment of the dialectic: the beautiful and the useful, the sacred and the economic, the lamp and the stubble. The dream is not abolished by the fire, but the dream is no longer the whole. There is here a practical spirit, however low, however unreflecting, however tied to nature and season. It is not freedom in the full sense, for it is not yet the freedom of the state in which the individual wills the universal as his own. But it is not mere inertia either.

Ramesh stands in the doorway with the accounts: cooking wage, groceries, electricity, all pressing on the day. I have in my pocket a hundred and sixty-six rupees. The household, like the state, is a body of particulars that demand satisfaction. The fire in Punjab and the unpaid wage at home are not the same, but they share a form: a need that has become visible, a law or duty that has not yet become actual. The CEC can only be removed through a process similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, while election commissioners can be removed by the president on the recommendation of the CEC. In the states and union territories, elections are supervised by a chief electoral officer, under the direction of the ECI. At the district and constituency levels, election-related work is carried out by the district election officers, electoral registration officers, and returning officers. The commission is responsible for the registration and recognition of political parties in the country. It prepares electoral rolls, and issues elector identification cards to eligible voters. It is also responsible for scrutinising candidates, allotting ballot symbols, enforcing the model code of conduct to be followed by the political parties and candidates, and monitoring election expenditure.

The Umpire Chosen by a Player

A newspaper speaks of 'the ECI's unfinished lessons'. I have read the headline and an account of what the Election Commission is. That is enough to begin, though not to judge the article.

In the last year of my first life I wrote against the English Reform Bill. My complaint was not that the English wished to count votes more fairly, but that they believed the counting of single heads was the whole of political right. A man casting a vote as an isolated atom, once in some years, for a candidate he does not know, does not experience himself as a member of the state; he experiences a lottery. I predicted indifference among the many and rule by those who organize them.

India counts more heads than any state has ever counted. What interests me is that it has not left the counting to the governing party, nor to the parties at all, but has made a third thing: a constitutional body that fixes the dates, keeps the rolls, issues the cards, recognizes the parties and allots their symbols, so that a man who cannot read may still choose, and watches what they spend. That is a real institution. It stands between the will of each and the government of all, and gives the bare act of voting a form, an office, a corps of officers down to every district. The atom is given a roll and a number. In this respect the Indians have answered part of my objection better than the English did in 1831.

But the account goes on. The commissioners are appointed by the president on the recommendation of a committee which the Prime Minister heads, with one minister of his choosing and the leader of the opposition. Two to one. The umpire is chosen by a committee in which one of the players holds the majority. The chief can be removed only as a judge of the Supreme Court is removed; his two colleagues can be removed on his recommendation. Independence is guarded at the top and not around it.

An institution exists to be trusted, and trust is not a feeling but a judgment about structure. Whatever lessons the article draws, and I will not guess at them, the unfinished part is likely here: a body that must stand above the parties is still constituted, in its appointment, by the strongest of them.

A constitution is grown, not made. This one is some seventy-five years old, young as constitutions go. It has grown an organ for counting. Whether that organ becomes a true member of the whole, and not an instrument of the head, is the next stage of its growth.
